title: How to Land 4,000 Planes During a Ground Stop
summary: For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out.Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extrao...
content:
For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out.

Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” some 4,000 airplanes were in the sky, headed for U.S. airports, according to Flightradar24, an aviation-tracking website. Even if no more flights took off, all of those planes needed to land.

For the people below, getting them down safely became an immediate preoccupation. This type of nationwide grounding had happened only twice before in recent history—once after the September 11 attacks, and once in January 2023 for about an hour and a half. Every aircraft still aloft needed to make it to its destination, despite apparently spotty communications.

Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. Pilots have emergency systems they can rely on if they lose radio communications, as well as onboard systems to detect where other aircraft are around them, R. John Hansman, the director of the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, told me. Communications problems don’t generally mean an immediate safety risk, and planes can still fly toward their destinations, he said. “The problem is getting them safely down.”

“The risk is related to how many other airplanes you could bump into,” he said. “So if you stop putting new airplanes into the system, then it becomes safer and safer and safer, until there’s no airplanes in the air. But of course, nobody’s flying, right?”

At the moment that the ground stop was declared, planes would have been landing. They landed in the minutes afterward, and in the hours after that. Within three hours, the number of flights still in the air had dropped to 550, Ian Petchenik, a spokesperson for Flightradar24, told me. Wheels hit the ground; the people on the plane and the people tracking their flights exhaled; pilots offered reassurances from the cockpit. On a plane that landed in Austin, carrying a number of writers headed a book festival (including some of my Atlantic colleagues), the pilot explained the delay on the tarmac by telling passengers there had been a “little issue with the FAA, folks, so no one is taking off and so there are no gates free.”

In the first hours, the Trump administration offered little immediate reassurance, or clarification of what had gone wrong or how long it might take to fix. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.” More than four hours after the outage began, Mullin told reporters at the White House that “we have seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack” but also did not rule it out or explain a cause for the outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who was on an airplane from Dallas amid the ground stop, said at the press conference that the country’s air traffic controllers faced “instability” in communications and radar—that switches and routers “actually got overwhelmed with data.” He blamed old analog equipment and software, and demanded $50 billion from Congress to fix the system. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he said.

Some of the problems, Duffy said, affected communications with the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, a network of 22 regional hubs. Airplanes communicate with these centers as they fly across the country. The disruption also affected what are known as Terminal Radar Approach Controls, facilities where air traffic controllers help guide planes approaching and departing airports. During this outage, air traffic controllers could apparently communicate on some radio frequencies but not others, and they had to actively search for ways to talk with the airplanes in the sky, Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told CNN. “This is not just a bad day,” he said. The air traffic controllers were “handling something that’s never been seen before.”

As the hours dragged on and planes kept landing but not taking off, the airports got crowded. Thousands of flights across the country got canceled. Passengers waited for hours, trying to figure out new plans, and scrambled for rental cars. They went home, or back to their hotels. Good Samaritans on social media offered rides. At Ronald Reagan National Airport, just outside Washington, D.C., hundreds of grounded travelers waited around a baggage carousel that moved so rarely that people felt comfortable sitting directly on it. Dana Johannesson, an ultrasound specialist in black scrubs and gold hoops, had gotten on her plane then gotten off, before waiting for her bags for hours; while she had sat on the plane, the American Airlines app still attributed the delay to the weather, but the pilot got on the loudspeaker to say that a friend had told him to give up on flying into Tampa and book himself a rental, she said.

Then the ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. Thousands of planes that had been flying four hours earlier had landed. But fewer than 400 were still in the air. The passengers on those planes got on and off their plane as planned. The system started up again, and the planes could take off.

Hana Kiros contributed reporting.

title: Scenes From the Nationwide Ground Stop
summary: On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare ground stop at all U.S. airports, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Across the country, departing flights were held for hours before the stop—attributed to a telecommunications outage—was lifted, dis...
content:
On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare ground stop at all U.S. airports, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Across the country, departing flights were held for hours before the stop—attributed to a telecommunications outage—was lifted, disrupting travel plans for some 1.5 million people. As planes start to take off again, thousands of passengers are still stuck on the ground.

title: The Next Major Grounding Will Be Worse
summary: Call me Dumb Nostradamus.Two days ago, I was on my friend Pablo Torre’s podcast to discuss some of my recent reporting on artificial intelligence. A lot of accomplished cybersecurity people I’ve spoken with are convinced that the combination of rapidly advancing AI systems, the diffusion of those sy...
content:
Call me Dumb Nostradamus.

Two days ago, I was on my friend Pablo Torre’s podcast to discuss some of my recent reporting on artificial intelligence. A lot of accomplished cybersecurity people I’ve spoken with are convinced that the combination of rapidly advancing AI systems, the diffusion of those systems via open-source models, and the rickety state of the world’s software will lead to something like rolling waves of chaos. Paraphrasing those experts, I told Pablo, “There’s going to be stuff that doesn’t work that disrupts your daily lives—and that’s the best you can hope for.”

That I learned all domestic flights in the United States were being grounded minutes after my own flight this evening landed—safely, and with the country’s chillest passengers and Delta crew—just goes to show that predicting chaos and being prepared for it are two very different skills.

To be clear, I have no idea what caused this. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a communications issue for interfering with air traffic control. It could be a classic software-upgrade face-palm; the extremely rare ground stop coincided with the FAA’s recent rollout of SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories), an $875 million AI-enhanced air-traffic-management system. The system’s maker, Air Space Intelligence, denies that its technology was at fault. Of course, the stop also coincided with yesterday’s Microsoft Outlook outage. That’s a lot of cyber smoke in two days.

Even if today has a boring explanation, the experts I’ve been talking with are pretty sure that plenty of days like this are coming, for two main reasons.

[Ian Bogost: Airport chaos began long before the ground stop]

First, anyone can be a bad guy now. Switching off a country’s power grid has technically been possible for a long time. What stopped anyone was the logic that kept the Cold War cold. The only people capable of that kind of chaos were governments, and governments know that turning off another country’s lights is exactly the sort of thing that gets answered with missiles. Deterrence works on parties who have something to lose and an address where you can send a reply. The trouble with AI (um, one of the troubles) is that it may hand state-grade capability to people who have neither.

You can’t deter a vandal. You don’t know who he is, and he doesn’t care, and he may currently be eating cereal in a gaming chair. The kids who used to grab a bat and swing at mailboxes can now grab some compute and turn off a town’s refrigerators—not for money or a cause, but because why not? Historically, that’s been the motive behind a great deal of human mischief.

Second, our best defense against this kind of chaos is amputation. None of the security people I’ve talked with has predicted an apocalypse. But they’re pretty convinced that the next 18 months are going to be a hassle, with regular disruptions to services that we rely on. That’s because when cyber defenders find a hole they can’t patch fast enough, the rational move is to amputate: Switch the system off and wait. Big institutions already do this, more quietly and more often than you’d think. Whatever caused today’s ground stop, halting every departure in the country “for reasons of safety” until someone works out what’s going on isn’t a sign that the system is failing. More and more, it is the system. I’ve just watched it from 22C.

You can do some things to protect yourself, but they fall into the realm of flossing: Install the update when your phone nags you, use passkeys instead of text-message codes, keep a little cash and water around. There’s some safety in numbers. Gmail and your giant bank are obvious targets, but they also employ armies of very serious, very well-paid people whose whole job is looking for trouble. And if they go down, hey, we’ll all have problems big enough that the world reading your love letters and poring over your credit-card statement will be the least of them.

The disorientation will be harder to adjust to. Most of us have been privileged to live in a world of peace, prosperity, and, above all, stability. We’ve gone to bed without having to wonder whether the traffic lights will work tomorrow. Now, if my sources are correct, we should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.

title: Of Course Americans Blamed the Ground Stop on AI
summary: For many hours, the Federal Aviation Administration did not explain why it issued a national ground stop in the United States this afternoon. The agency described the cause only as a “telecommunications outage” and cited “extraordinary circumstances,” but failed to say more. So speculation abounded:...
content:
For many hours, the Federal Aviation Administration did not explain why it issued a national ground stop in the United States this afternoon. The agency described the cause only as a “telecommunications outage” and cited “extraordinary circumstances,” but failed to say more. So speculation abounded: Was the problem connected with the onboarding of a new AI route-selection system this week? Is it somehow related to the Microsoft Outlook outage this week? Or is the cause some antiquated telecommunications system that just finally gave up trying?

In the absence of solid information from trusted authorities, people interpret crises through the prism of their preexisting concerns. When the aviation system shut down, many Americans’ minds went to DOGE cuts, cyberattacks by hostile foreign actors, recent reports of renegade AI. A safety planner’s job is to envision the full range of possible threats and assess how likely each one is to occur. Even before recent advances in artificial intelligence, the list of factors that could jeopardize commercial aviation was already long: terrorism, extreme weather, staffing strains, the decay of outdated communications networks, and more. AI could theoretically help the aviation system manage risks and disruptions, but it also adds many more variables that could go wrong.

It’s no wonder many Americans were quick to envision rogue disruption caused by the new technology: When AI CEOs tell us that the risk of AI is so great that it is essentially uninsurable, people take notice.

The more prosaic reality is that America’s crucial infrastructure systems are built without sufficient resiliency. As a result, a single disruption can have national consequences. CNN reported tonight that the aviation problem may have originated with network routers at Chicago’s Midway airport. In a fragile system, glitches spread unpredictably and potentially rapidly. So far, more than 10,000 flights have been disrupted.

Fortunately, our aviation-safety systems had sufficient backups to let planes land safely, and pilots have been communicating through emergency-frequency lines. The best analogy is a spare tire: It’s good enough to get you to the nearest gas station but not much farther.

The ground stop—which has now been lifted—has exposed either a new security vulnerability or a problem with old systems; either way, the economic impact could well be major. The high stakes are all the more reason that, in moments of crisis, authorities should quickly tell the public what is known, what is not known, and what they are doing to close the information gap. Finally, after four hours, the Trump administration held a press conference, at which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “things seem to be working, as we can say, in the right direction.” How long it will take for the mess at airports to clear is anyone’s guess.

title: Airport Chaos Began Long Before the Ground Stop
summary: Every civilian airplane in the United States has been told not to fly, owing to a nationwide FAA ground stop. As I write this, very little is known about the nature of the safety risk or the issue underlying it.According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, “a communication issue impacting all Ai...
content:
Every civilian airplane in the United States has been told not to fly, owing to a nationwide FAA ground stop. As I write this, very little is known about the nature of the safety risk or the issue underlying it.

According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” necessitated the action, which was undertaken for reasons of safety. The stop could keep planes on the ground for hours, or much longer. Even when the stop ends, unwinding the inevitable backup will take more time. If you’re in the air, your plane will land. But if you are at the airport waiting for one, it might be best to give up and go home.

In a sense, chaos such as this arrived long before today. Air travel has become terrible, and it has done so slowly and over a long period of time. In terms of safety, air travel is far less dangerous than driving, although an erosion of oversight, funding, infrastructure, and other factors might be changing that. James Fallows, a longtime contributor to The Atlantic, just wrote a lengthy article for The New York Times Magazine about exactly this risk. Setting aside actual safety, the experience of traveling by commercial airline has been getting worse and worse for years.

Once blue with clarity, the American skies are now clouded with uncertainty. Risk and failure are now presumed. My son’s flight from Boston to LaGuardia was delayed earlier today, before the ground stop, by weather. “You should have taken the train,” I texted him. He made it out mere hours before all planes were grounded. New York City–area airports have suffered delays in recent days due to weather—a seemingly constant issue flying in or out of that city. My son and his sister, who both live in Manhattan, decided months ago not to even try to leave town for Thanksgiving, because delays and cancellations have become so commonplace.

The reasons are many. Industry consolidation reduced routes to medium-size cities, sending more passengers through a smaller number of hubs. Passengers might have to make connections for routes that once flew direct, or drive longer distances to reach a bigger airport. Extreme weather has worsened flying conditions headed into and out of almost any airport, making arrivals and departures less reliable. Delays and disruptions can mean that equipment and crews don’t arrive for a flight on time or at all. Even when the planes and pilots are available, the Air Route Traffic Control Centers are more sparsely staffed than they once were, while the number of flights each one manages has increased.

The ARTCCs are FAA facilities distributed around the country, each one responsible for guiding aircraft through a specific region’s airspace. For example, the Chicago center handles northern Illinois and parts of Wisconsin, Iowa, Indiana, and Michigan. That center might hand off traffic bound for Dallas to the Kansas City center, or to Indianapolis for planes en route to Atlanta. What airport-control towers do for takeoff and landing, these centers do for the cruising portion of a flight—keeping aircraft safely spaced out from one another by assigning them altitudes or by guiding pilots around weather.

On the internet, where citizens seem to revel in conspiracism, some people have connected today’s FAA ground stop with yesterday’s Microsoft Outlook outage—and the murky notion that advanced AI models might be responsible for both, and more. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at a news conference that a cyberattack is unlikely to have caused the ground stop. Even so, a Government Accountability Office report from September identified threats in certain aspects of FAA communication systems that malicious actors could, in principle, exploit. And just yesterday, the FAA expanded the use of an AI-based air-traffic-management tool to all 22 control centers.

The controllers on the ground may not know much about the cause yet, either. “We lost all of our approach frequencies, and other facilities did too,” an air traffic controller based in the Midwest told The Atlantic. “For this to be affecting multiple facilities nationwide doesn’t make any sort of sense.” Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport has run out of tarmac space already, causing planes to be diverted elsewhere, the controller added. “This is going to be a mess for days, if not weeks.”

Whatever the cause, once the delays inevitably happen, even big, newer airports often become inhospitable hosts. Long walks through huge hubs now feel required. Limited seating at gates makes waits of any kind uncomfortable. Frequent fliers don’t fare much better, because long queues to get into overcrowded lounges have turned those spots into marginally less horrible waiting rooms (albeit ones that also offer free cheese). The frequent traveling that would formerly have gotten you into those lounges (or upgraded to first class after leaving them, should your flight actually depart) has become optional; the airlines have found that travelers are willing to pay for those perks instead, or earn them by spending money with their airline-branded credit cards. Customer service can be truculent or impossible, requiring long telephone wait times, confusing and unreliable apps, or the traversal of even more airport hallways to self-service kiosks—none of which are guaranteed to produce results. The entire experience of flying is adversarial.

When travelers do get disrupted, like so many have been today and will be this weekend (and perhaps subsequently), they are likely to get limited assistance from the airlines, which now have more limited incentives to help and reduced consequences for failing to do so. This ground stop is not the airlines’ fault, but travelers have become inured to being treated badly no matter the cause of their travel headaches. Almost exactly a year ago, the Department of Transportation withdrew initiatives that the Biden administration had put in place to require compensation, meals, lodging, and rebooking for airline-caused disruptions, such as equipment failures. Penalties for failing to accommodate passengers also began to fall away, in favor of voluntary compliance and faith in capitalism-driven competition—even though only four major airlines (American, Delta, Southwest, and United) now account for more than three-quarters of U.S. airline seats.

Eventually, and perhaps soon, Americans will learn more about the cause of today’s nationwide ground stop. According to CNN, some airlines were told that network-router problems at Chicago Midway had cascaded nationwide, but that proximate issue might suggest different ultimate causes. Even after the cause becomes known, let alone put on the path to remedy, the deep and seemingly permanent misery of commercial flight in the United States will still roar into the air above it.

summary: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African...
content:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

content:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo

Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

content:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
